description: Roughly 30% of work permits have been delivered in exchange for a brokerage fee of NIS 1,500-2,500. The Bank of Israel put broker profits at NIS 122 million in 2018. That year, 45% of the 94,254 Palestinian workers in Israel got their jobs through agents, who could take up to a third of a worker's wages.
energy_note: A third of the wage, to be allowed to earn it.

description: Workers reported paying around NIS 2,500 - about USD 688 - for documents obtained through dishonest means, often nearly half their total income, paid out of pocket. Kav LaOved documented monthly fees of NIS 1,500-3,500 per worker.
energy_note: Half your pay, to the man who sold you the paper.

description: One middleman alone issued permits for 200 workers at NIS 2,000-3,000 each per month, and was one link in a chain; most of the money reportedly ended up with former Israeli security personnel closer to those issuing permits. Contractors hold quotas they do not need and resell permits for around NIS 2,000 after paying NIS 1,400.
energy_note: A quota, bought at 1,400 and sold at 2,000.

aspect: The reform did not end it
description: A new system adopted in 2020 was meant to end the black market and did not end the role of agents. The ITUC has called for ILO fair recruitment standards under which recruitment fees are not borne by workers.
Some 100,000 Palestinians had permits revoked after October 2023. A former Tulkarem job-placement operator says Palestinian brokers now charge more than triple the pre-war price.

aspect: The whole arrangement is invisible in the wage statistics
description: Recorded earnings look like a wage. The worker's actual take-home is that minus a third, and no dataset of Palestinian incomes subtracts it.
energy_note: Every income figure for this group is overstated.
